To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that
the genetic make‐up of the individuals participating in weight loss trials is a key factor to consider in the design of future studies.
the genetic background of an individual could affect the response to weight loss interventions.
(1) the individual genetic make‐‐up participates in energy expenditure regulation (2) appetite control (3) lipid metabolism and (4) adipogenesis.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the study of genetic polymorphisms and weight loss prognosis in response to dietary interventions.
the identification of the genetic factors involved in the response of obese individuals to weight‐loss interventions.
the study of the genetic component in the response to a diet and/or physical activity intervention.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
genetic factors are involved in weight loss prognosis.
there is not enough evidence to support the existence of an important genetic component in weight loss prognosis.
the individual genetic profile could be used as a predictive factor of weight loss prognosis in some individuals, but not all.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
the genetic make‐up is an important component of the individual response to weight loss, but it is still too early to predict weight loss success or failure based on a genetic profile.
the genetic background of the patient could be a useful tool to predict the success of the weight‐loss treatment.
genetic polymorphisms may be used to improve the prediction of the response to weight loss interventions.
The main takeaway from our work is that
the genetic background of an individual may influence the response to weight loss interventions and, thus, the prognosis of weight reduction.
there is no single gene that predicts the outcome of a weight loss programme.
there is no single genetic marker that can predict the outcome of a weight loss intervention.
